claims.summary: The frozen unit places pre-deployment preparation before schema execution. That can prepare an existing table, but the stated first deployment creates this table in the schema plan, so the reference data cannot be populated at that earlier point.

The unit's failure warning concerns plain INSERT replay, not every use of INSERT. The repaired option now explicitly excludes existing-key checks and updates and replays the full set. It fails the retained-key and changed-value contract; a one-time empty target or a separately guarded missing-key-only workflow has different requirements.

The unit runs versioned reference-data scripts after schema execution and demonstrates updating matched rows and inserting missing keys. That pattern supplies the required initial ordering and convergence. Equivalent correct reconciliation code is permitted; MERGE is not the exclusive implementation.

The declarative schema model does not populate required lookup values; the source introduces data scripts specifically for that purpose. A schema-only deployment fits a contract with separate data provisioning, not this deployment's required reference-data convergence.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reread the actual frozen reference-data unit, not its curator summary. It separates object definitions from versioned row data, places seeding after schema-plan execution, and explains that post-deployment scripts run repeatedly. Its example updates matched reference values and inserts missing keys. The warning concerns plain INSERT replay, not every INSERT-based implementation; this review does not promote MERGE as mandatory or infer concurrency safety or whole-deployment atomicity.

choiceReviews.rationale: The first schema plan creates the lookup table, so a reference-data script executed before that plan has no such table to populate. Existing-table preparation could use the earlier hook, but independently creating the table there would introduce a different, unstated schema-authoring workflow.

B now expressly limits the workflow to unconditional replay of the full set and prohibits existing-row checking or updating. It cannot update changed values for retained keys and supplies none of the documented existing/missing-row reconciliation. The prior guarded-INSERT interpretation is explicitly excluded; moreover missing-key-only insertion would not satisfy the newly stated value-update requirement. The rejection does not depend on claiming every possible INSERT must raise an error.

Post-deployment reconciliation runs after initial table creation and can bring retained rows to the current reference values while inserting missing keys. The unit's matched UPDATE and not-matched INSERT example directly demonstrates these two required operations. C names the strategy rather than insisting on one particular DML implementation.

The declarative schema model describes table objects; the source introduces separate data scripts because it does not populate or update the required lookup values. Schema-only deployment would fit externally provisioned data, but the stem assigns versioned row convergence to this deployment itself.

claims.summary: The pre/post product article separates calculation from execution, and the compare-project article generates deployment SQL from the current target. Completing a prerequisite before that generation makes its resulting schema an input. The testing unit supports validating the full sequence on a dedicated target, not assuming ordering proves safety.

PreDeploy is a real supported deployment hook, but the source explicitly places plan calculation before it executes. This workflow is useful for compatible preparation before plan execution; it does not change the target schema used in that already completed calculation.
PostDeploy is a real supported hook that runs after the deployment plan completes. It can handle post-schema work, but cannot supply a prerequisite schema state needed when that plan is calculated.

Generating and reviewing a saved deployment script is supported. That artifact represents the target state used at generation, however; performing a separate prerequisite afterward does not automatically regenerate it. The workflow can suit compatible intervening preparation, not a requirement to calculate from the new schema.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reread the opening product contract and project-item examples. The deployment plan is calculated before PreDeploy executes; PreDeploy then precedes plan execution, and PostDeploy follows completion. These are actual stage boundaries, not filename rules. The article also excludes pre/post scripts from object-model validation, so correct ordering alone is not implementation-safety proof.

Reread Deploy report and Review deployment T-SQL scripts in the actual frozen article. Plan/report generation compares the source model with the connected target, and Script materializes the target-specific T-SQL for later review and execution. A prerequisite completed before this generation can change the input schema; executing a previously generated file does not itself request a fresh comparison.

Reread the testing-level and integration sections. Structural builds do not establish runtime correctness; multi-operation integration tests use a deployed dedicated database and known state. This supports the explanation's requirement to validate the prerequisite and full sequence on the isolated target, not a guarantee that the selected ordering makes any migration safe.

choiceReviews.rationale: Completing the prerequisite first means the later source-to-target comparison reads its resulting schema. Generating, reviewing and executing the script afterward therefore meets the specific planning-input requirement. The proposed order remains subject to the explanation's separate validation of actual schema and data effects.

A supported PreDeploy hook executes before the schema plan runs, but only after that plan has been calculated. Including it in the generated combined script does not execute its prerequisite while the comparison is reading the target. This workflow can perform preparation compatible with an already calculated plan, not supply the required new comparison state.

The documented PostDeploy hook executes after the schema plan, so it is later still than plan calculation. It is suitable for tasks such as populating objects after their creation, but cannot make a prerequisite schema mutation visible to the calculation that generated that same plan.

The saved script is generated and reviewed before the prerequisite changes the target. Running the prerequisite before executing the saved file changes execution conditions but does not regenerate that file from a new comparison. A previously approved script may remain valid after compatible preparation; that possibility does not meet this explicit requirement to calculate from the changed schema.
